title: Learning with, rather than through, AI: co-designing science education for critical AI literacy
extended_summary:
This opinion paper addresses how generative AI, especially tools like ChatGPT, is changing science education and science communication. The central question is not whether AI should be used in schools, but how teachers can keep students engaged in critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and disciplinary understanding when AI can instantly provide answers, explanations, and writing support.

The paper argues for a shift from learning through AI to learning with AI. It proposes that teachers should treat generative AI as a classroom tool to be used deliberately, with students learning to question outputs, verify claims, and reflect on bias, misinformation, and academic integrity. The author emphasizes teacher agency, human judgment, and participatory pedagogy, where students help co-design norms for ethical AI use.

The context is mainly science education, especially high school classrooms, though the discussion is conceptual rather than based on a new empirical intervention. Examples include using ChatGPT for pre-lesson explanations, critique of AI-generated answers, debate activities, and guided reflection. The conclusion is that AI should augment, not replace, teachers, and that critical AI literacy should become part of science curricula so students can engage responsibly and thoughtfully with AI-rich learning environments.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a 2025 opinion article and not an empirical study. It offers conceptual arguments and cites other work, but it does not present a new research design, sample, or original outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially meaningful influence on practice and policy by framing how teachers should integrate generative AI, but it does not demonstrate measured impact in a study sample. Its practical implications are broad yet remain theoretical rather than evidenced in this article.

interventions.use_case: Discusses ChatGPT and similar generative AI chatbots as classroom knowledge brokers, student explanation tools, and teacher assistants for drafting quizzes, worksheets, lesson plans, and feedback; emphasizes guided, critical use in science education.

finding.finding_summary: This opinion piece argues that generative AI can either undermine or strengthen durable skills depending on how it is used. The article cites prior studies and reports suggesting possible reductions in critical thinking and brain engagement with uncritical ChatGPT use, while advocating structured classroom use to promote metacognition, evidence evaluation, and critical AI literacy; no new effect size is reported in this paper.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, and evidence-evaluation skills discussed conceptually; no direct empirical measure in this paper

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can support scientific reasoning when students use ChatGPT to explain concepts, detect errors, and critique AI-generated responses, but can also weaken reasoning if students outsource thinking to the tool. This is an opinion/review piece and does not report a primary empirical effect size or sample for scientific reasoning outcomes.
finding.measure: Scientific reasoning, conceptual understanding, error detection in science tasks; discussed through classroom examples

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teachers who use AI say it saves time on tasks such as preparing worksheets, quizzes, and lesson plans, and that it can improve the quality of adapting materials and providing feedback. The article cites a report in which about 80% of U.S. teachers using AI said it saved time and about 60% said it improved their work quality, but those figures are secondary citations rather than original study results in this paper.
finding.measure: Teacher time savings and perceived quality of planning/adapting materials and feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is normative and institutional: it argues for ethical AI integration, guided-use policies, and participatory pedagogy in science education. It does not estimate a quantitative institutional effect, but it frames AI literacy and teacher agency as system-level responses to widespread student access to generative AI.
finding.measure: Policy and pedagogical recommendations for school/institutional AI integration
